summary: Describes a possible mechanism for controlling the rate of acknowledgment traffic in TCP, using cooperation between the data sender and receiver. It is aimed at links where the return path is constrained. It is informational and does not define a standard.

eli5.summary: Receivers send back little messages saying they got the data, and on a slow road these notes can clog the way back. This idea has sender and receiver agree to send fewer notes when the road is crowded.

subtitle: Reducing acknowledgement traffic during reverse-path congestion.

tldr.problem: TCP receivers send many acknowledgement packets on the return path, which can cause congestion and slow down data transfer when the return path is heavily loaded.
tldr.mechanism: The sender detects lost acknowledgement packets and tells the receiver to send fewer ACKs by reducing the frequency (the ACK Ratio), sending one ACK for every R data packets instead of one per packet or pair.
tldr.outcome: This mechanism is informational and has not been standardized, but it provides a way to relieve congestion on return paths and prevent acknowledgement traffic from blocking data transmission.

facts.label: Minimum ACK Rate
facts.value: At least 2 ACKs per window of 4 segments

facts.label: Adjustment rule for loss
facts.value: Double the ACK Ratio per round-trip time with congestion event

today: RFC 5690 is informational and has not been standardized or widely deployed. It remains a proposal for potential use in networks with heavily congested reverse paths, and the research and implementation communities are encouraged to evaluate it further.

sections.title: The Acknowledgement Congestion Problem
sections.content: In TCP, the receiver sends acknowledgement packets (ACKs) back to the sender to confirm receipt of data. On networks with asymmetric or congested reverse paths, these acknowledgement packets can themselves become a bottleneck, causing the sender to slow down even though data packets have room to travel. This document proposes a mechanism to reduce ACK traffic when the return path is congested, based on similar mechanisms already used in DCCP's CCID 2 profile.
sections.eli5: ACKs are thank-you notes the receiver sends back. Too many thank-you notes can jam up the return road and make everything slow.

sections.title: How ACK Congestion Control Works
sections.content:
The mechanism requires both the sender and receiver to participate. During connection setup, they negotiate support using a new TCP option called the ACK Congestion Control Permitted option. The sender monitors arriving ACKs for signs of congestion (lost or ECN-marked packets). When congestion is detected, the sender sends the receiver a new ACK Ratio value using another new TCP option, the ACK Ratio option. An ACK Ratio of R means the receiver should send approximately one ACK for every R data packets received instead of the normal one ACK per one or two packets. The receiver implements this by maintaining a counter: when the counter reaches R, it sends an ACK and resets the counter.

The default initial ACK Ratio is two, so receivers acknowledge at least every other data packet. When the sender detects an ACK loss or ECN mark, it doubles the ratio to reduce ACK traffic further. When the sender observes a period free of ACK congestion events, it gradually decreases the ACK Ratio by one, allowing more frequent ACKs again.
sections.eli5: The sender and receiver agree on a number. The receiver sends one thank-you note for every R packages. When the return road gets crowded, the sender makes R bigger; when it clears up, R gets smaller.

sections.title: TCP Options and Implementation
sections.content: Two new TCP options enable the mechanism. The ACK Congestion Control Permitted option is sent only on packets with the SYN bit set during connection establishment. It signals that the sender or receiver supports ACK congestion control. The ACK Ratio option is sent on data packets by the sender to communicate the new ratio value to the receiver. Because data packets use reliable delivery in TCP, the sender knows when the receiver has acknowledged a packet carrying an ACK Ratio option and thus received the new ratio. This allows the sender to change the ACK Ratio by at most one step per round-trip time: it can either double the ratio (halving the ACK rate) or decrease it by one (increasing the ACK rate). The receiver must respect the ACK Ratio but can always send an ACK if a delayed ACK timer expires, ensuring no acknowledgements are withheld indefinitely.
sections.eli5: Two small tags in the TCP packet say "I support this" and "use ratio 4." The sender changes the ratio slowly so it knows the receiver got the message.

sections.title: Detecting Loss and Adjusting Ratios
sections.content: The sender infers an ACK packet has been lost when it receives an acknowledgement that covers more than R additional data packets, without a preceding acknowledgement covering a subset of those packets. This inference relies on the sender's knowledge of the ACK Ratio. During periods of data packet loss (detected via timeout or fast retransmit), the sender stops attempting to detect ACK loss, because irregular acknowledgement jumps during recovery make loss inference unreliable. For each round-trip time with an ACK congestion event, the sender doubles the ACK Ratio. For multiple consecutive round-trip times without congestion events, the sender decreases the ratio by one. The sender must also respect constraints: the ratio is always at least two (except when the congestion window is very small), and it is limited to prevent the receiver from acknowledging fewer than two ACKs per window of at least four full-sized segments. These rules aim to maintain a sending rate for ACKs that is roughly TCP-friendly, balancing load reduction with responsiveness.
sections.eli5: If the thank-you note is missing, send bigger numbers. If thank-you notes keep arriving, slowly make the number smaller. Keep it sensible: the receiver always sends at least two notes per window.

sections.title: Challenges and Open Questions
sections.content: The mechanism faces several complications in real deployments. Delayed acknowledgements—where the receiver sends one ACK for multiple packets instead of one per packet—can cause false negatives, where the sender misses detecting an ACK loss. Two-way traffic complicates loss inference: if the receiver sends a pure ACK followed by a data packet with the same acknowledgement number, a lost pure ACK may go undetected. Reordering of ACK packets on the return path requires careful design to avoid false loss inferences. In environments where ACK traffic does not significantly contribute to congestion but is still dropped, ACK congestion control may hurt the connection without helping overall network load. TCP implementations that skip ACKs (sending one ACK for a burst of packets) undermine the mechanism's assumptions. The document identifies these issues and suggests that implementation and testing will be needed to determine how serious each complication is and whether workarounds are necessary.
sections.eli5: Some tricky situations can confuse the system: when receivers skip thank-yous, when the road is messy, or when too many rules collide. The document says we need to test and see what works.

sections.title: Security and Incentives
sections.content: Because ACK congestion control is optional, neither endpoint is forced to use it. As long as it remains optional and not standardized, there is little incentive for endpoints to cheat. A sender cannot force a receiver to use ACK congestion control, and a receiver cannot force a sender to send ACK Ratio options. However, if combined with ECN-capable ACK packets, some scenarios emerge where endpoints might cheat: for example, a sender could avoid reducing the ACK Ratio even when ACKs are ECN-marked. The document raises questions about the incentives and avenues for cheating but does not resolve them, noting that further analysis is needed as the mechanism matures.
sections.eli5: Since both sides choose to use this, nobody has a reason to cheat. But if someone does cheat, the system still works—it just won't help as much.
